content: 1. Radiographic evidence of cavitation and prior treatment with first-line and second-line tuberculosis (TB) drugs were considered in the analysis. Patients with extensively drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB) were excluded from the aggregated data meta-analysis whenever possible. 2. A total of 61 cohorts provided end-of-treatment outcome data. Among these, 23 cohorts used standardized treatment regimens, while 38 cohorts employed individualized therapy, introducing a potential risk of confounding by indication. 3. Of the 61 cohorts, 18 did not specify which second-line injectable agent was used. Consequently, only the remaining 43 cohorts were included in this analysis. 4. There was potential confounding due to the preferential inclusion of capreomycin in individualized regimens for patients with more advanced resistance patterns or disease severity. 5. Amikacin or kanamycin was used in nearly all studies. Comparisons were made between studies where 72%–100% of patients received these injectable agents (intervention group) versus studies where 0%–71% of patients received them (comparator group). 6. Adjusted treatment success proportions were reported as follows: 94% (95% CI: 90%–97%) 89% (95% CI: 83%–96%) 82% (95% CI: 75%–88%) 78% (95% CI: 70%–86%) 92% (95% CI: 87%–97%) 93% (95% CI: 86%–97%) 77% (95% CI: 69%–84%) 83% (95% CI: 76%–89%) 7. Serious adverse events (SAEs) reported in patients were attributed to specific medications by unblinded authors using non-standardized methods to define, ascertain, and report these events. Valid comparisons with patients not receiving the target medication were not possible, as SAEs in these patients could be attributed to other drugs administered concurrently. 8. The use of ethionamide/prothionamide was compared to regimens without these drugs in adults with rifampicin-resistant TB or multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB). This analysis combined data from 32 observational studies, most of which involved individualized treatment regimens, introducing risks of selection bias and confounding by indication. 9. Cycloserine and terizidone were analyzed together for their effects on treatment outcomes in MDR-TB. No regional differences were observed. However, SAEs were attributed to these drugs by unblinded authors using non-standardized methods, limiting valid comparisons with patients not receiving these medications. 10. Linezolid was evaluated for its efficacy and safety in treating MDR-TB and XDR-TB. The intervention group received an initial dose of 1200 mg/day for 4–6 weeks, followed by 300–600 mg/day. Adverse events were reported inconsistently across studies, with risks of allocation and ascertainment bias due to lack of blinding and unclear randomization methods. 11. Clofazimine was assessed for its role in MDR-TB treatment. Outcomes were compared between patients receiving clofazimine and those not receiving Group 5 drugs. Adjusted estimates were derived using propensity score matching. However, the evidence was limited by risks of bias, including confounding by indication, and inconsistent reporting of adverse events. 12. Across all analyses, the certainty of evidence was often rated as very low due to methodological limitations, including small sample sizes, lack of blinding, and risks of bias in observational studies.
